{"id": "2:45/q11", "question": "To what does the feminine pronoun in وَإِنَّهَا refer?", "turns_on": "Whether grammar favors a nearby expressed noun, an implied action, both coordinated nouns, the wider discourse, or a contextually inferred matter.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q11/p1", "position": "Prayer alone.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Abu Hayyan, al-Tabari as relayed by Ibn Kathir, and Alusi favor the nearer feminine noun. Others stress prayer's prominence, universal obligation, superiority, or inclusion of many kinds of patience; 9:34 and 62:11 offer analogies, though al-Samin questions 62:11 because it uses aw. Qurtubi adds that prayer engages all limbs and desires, making it heavier than fasting. Samarrai ties the return to prayer to the prior command in 2:43. Tabari rejects an unsupported hidden referent and maintains the apparent sense."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p2", "position": "The act of seeking help through the two practices.", "reasons": "Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl and others derive the verbal noun from استعينوا; Jishumi calls it the most apparent general antecedent, Tabarsi adduces a poetic adjective with implied abstract noun, and Alusi rebuts the claim that seeking help cannot be burdensome. Bursevi chooses it."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p3", "position": "Each of patience and prayer distributively, or both together under a singular form.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash's distributive reading invokes Mary and her son as one sign (23:50); Baghawi adds the two gardens (18:33), and poets use singular predicates. Others explain dominance, ellipsis, or inclusion of the first item in the second by 9:62. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin object that wāw normally requires dual agreement, unlike aw; al-Samin rejects this joint reading."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p4", "position": "The whole preceding set of commands and prohibitions or admonition.", "reasons": "Kashshaf traces it back to 'Remember My favor'; Razi and Baydawi allow it, and Ibn Ashur prefers this widest, most inclusive referent while allowing all three main possibilities. Study Quran notes day and night attention."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p5", "position": "Worship or self-discipline implied by patience and prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi propose worship; Jishumi adds self-discipline and 'what came before.' Al-Samin lists worship as an understood antecedent."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p6", "position": "Responding to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Mawardi reports it, al-Asamm and al-Akhfash are named by later sources; Ibn Atiyya says the text gives no evidence, Jishumi says it is neither named nor uniquely implied, and Alusi considers preceding commands closer."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p7", "position": "The Kaaba or changed qibla implied by prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Muqatil are reported for this; Ibn Atiyya calls it weaker than responding to Muhammad, and Alusi calls it still less likely than the broad prior-command referent."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p8", "position": "An implicit deed or offense.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim's implicit 'this deed' or 'this offense' appears in Jishumi and Tabarsi; Tabarsi rejects omitted antecedents as contextually unmentioned."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p9", "position": "The instruction to persevere in both practices.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares traits or instructions referred to by feminine pronouns in 28:80 and 41:34–35."}, {"id": "2:45/q11/p10", "position": "Angels, in a context-truncated report.", "reasons": "Zarkashi records Qatada's identification but says the already-mentioned antecedent fits better."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q12", "question": "What grammatical form is 'وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q12/p1", "position": "Inna takes the pronoun as its noun and kabīra as predicate; the emphatic lām is attached to the predicate.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi note possible masculine forms outside Qur'anic recitation; Tabarsi says the lām moves to the predicate to distinguish it from inna, unlike other sisters of inna. Razi shows an understood noun can receive an implicit pronoun, citing 16:61."}, {"id": "2:45/q12/p2", "position": "A singular predicate may serve one or both coordinated nouns by attraction, ellipsis, or distribution.", "reasons": "Akhfash distinguishes wāw, normally joint, from aw, selecting one and usually the nearer; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin contest use of aw parallels for wāw. Poems of Ibn Ahmar, Burjumi, Hassan and anonymous poets, plus 9:34, 9:62, 23:50 and 62:11, furnish examples."}, {"id": "2:45/q12/p3", "position": "The exception has an implicit negative: the act is not light except to the humble.", "reasons": "Al-Samin attaches على الخاشعين to كبيرة; Abu Hayyan calls the exception complete. Zarkashi says illa can follow positive wording with negative meaning or a statement made true by the exception."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q13", "question": "What does لَكَبِيرَةٌ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective describes general difficulty, a particular historical demand, or the greatness of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q13/p1", "position": "Heavy, arduous, or psychologically difficult.", "reasons": "Tabari, Dahhak, Hasan, Wahidi, Jishumi, Zamakhshari and others explain physical size or weight as a metaphor for difficulty, comparing 42:13; Ibn Ashur also cites 2:143 and 6:35. Abu Hayyan distinguishes the sense from size and age; Harali notes magnitude or rank, outward or inward, while Biqai reads prayer's greatness as divine orientation."}, {"id": "2:45/q13/p2", "position": "For the Jews and hypocrites, the concrete burden was the qibla change from Jerusalem to the Kaaba.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Jaddi ibn Akhtab and Sa'id ibn Amr the poet among the Jews; other versions mention Jews and hypocrites. Believing humble people did not resist it."}, {"id": "2:45/q13/p3", "position": "For polytheists, Muhammad's summons to prayer and faith felt like a great demand.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd reports their words; Zajjaj and Wahidi say prayer joined to faith in the Prophet weighed on unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q14", "question": "Why is it light for the humble, and heavy for others?", "turns_on": "Whether ease comes from expected reward, trained disposition, divine help, or communion, and whether ease threatens the basis for merit.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q14/p1", "position": "Belief in reward, judgment, and benefit makes the effort bearable.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi, Tabarsi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, Ibn Ashur and others compare bitter medicine accepted for its cure; hypocrites and showoffs expect no benefit. Razi rejects the inference that deeper bodily and inward engagement makes it harder for the humble. Ibn Kathir says they know they will meet and return to God. The Prophet called prayer the coolness or delight of his eyes even while praying until his feet swelled."}, {"id": "2:45/q14/p2", "position": "Humility and habituation make service congenial and release attachment to status.", "reasons": "Tabarsi says the humble have habituated themselves to prayer and can lose rank to gain faith; Ibn Ashur says a disciplined soul rests in God's command. Elmalili says practice becomes pleasure. Qurtubi's spiritual teachers invoke eternal election, while Ibn Kathir quotes divine easing."}, {"id": "2:45/q14/p3", "position": "Intimate communion or divine self-disclosure eclipses the experienced burden.", "reasons": "Qushayri's transmitted saying links manifestation and humility; he distinguishes toil in ongoing obedience from union and nearness through witnessing and says God eases overpowering unveilings so service resumes. Sulami's authorities speak of bowed heart, secret and limbs; Qashani of tender hearts receiving subtle lights; Bursevi says absorption in converse with God makes hardship unfelt."}, {"id": "2:45/q14/p4", "position": "The objection is that the humble should bear more, since they engage body and inner faculties more fully.", "reasons": "Razi records the argument from engaged body, heart, hearing and sight and responses to warnings and promises; he answers that difficulty concerns those without confidence in reward or punishment."}, {"id": "2:45/q14/p5", "position": "A further objection asks how an unburdened act can merit reward.", "reasons": "Jishumi raises this difficulty without an explicit answer in the note."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q15", "question": "Who are the ٱلْخَٰشِعِينَ?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is an inclusive quality or identifies a particular class or persons.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q15/p1", "position": "Believers, especially those who affirm God's revelation and the return to Him.", "reasons": "Mujahid calls them true believers; Ibn Abbas adds assent to revelation. Muqatil links belief to certainty of meeting God and recompense. Tabarsi compares acceptance of bitter medicine when cure is known. The reports about Ali and companions give a more particular identification elsewhere."}, {"id": "2:45/q15/p2", "position": "Those who fear God or His force and warnings.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya, Hasan, al-Asamm, and Ibn Zayd use fear or awe; Ibn Zayd cites 42:45. Qatada locates the fear in the heart and lowered gaze in prayer; Dahhak joins fear to obedience and affirming promises and threats."}, {"id": "2:45/q15/p3", "position": "The meek, lowly, submissive, and obedient.", "reasons": "Tabari joins humility, obedience and fear; Zajjaj says they respond without clinging to leadership; Warraq and Abu Rawq specify obedient worshippers. Muqatil ibn Hayyan calls them meek. Ibn Ashur describes self-discipline and attention to future consequences."}, {"id": "2:45/q15/p4", "position": "Those who pray.", "reasons": "A saying attributed to Ibn Abbas makes the definition specifically worshippers in prayer."}, {"id": "2:45/q15/p5", "position": "The Messenger and Ali, in an inward or transmitted identification.", "reasons": "Abu al-Hasan identifies them as submissive and attentive in prayer and names the Messenger and Ali; al-Baqir separately reports revelation concerning Ali, Uthman ibn Maz'

{"id": "2:45/q16", "question": "What is the meaning and range of khushūʿ?", "turns_on": "How its inward, bodily, vocal and visual senses relate, especially in comparison with khuḍūʿ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q16/p1", "position": "Humility, lowering, quietness, stillness, or submission.", "reasons": "Tabari cites humbled mountains in a poem; Wahidi traces still voices (20:108), collapsed wall, barren land (41:39), drooping hump and lowered eyes, with al-Nabigha's poetry. Zajjaj likens it to a deserted house; Qurtubi adds low land, obscure town and quiet voices; Ibn Ashur's al-Nabigha image is a worn trough rim. Jishumi reports Ibn Durayd's synonyms and dialectal sense of bowing. Biqai's Harali includes still limbs and thoughts."}, {"id": "2:45/q16/p2", "position": "Khushūʿ reaches voice and sight as well as the body; khuḍūʿ chiefly denotes bodily submission.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Tabarsi, al-Layth and al-Samin draw this distinction; Tabarsi adds softened or lowered gaze, voice and bowed head. Abu Hayyan cites the Kaaba as a low mound on water."}, {"id": "2:45/q16/p3", "position": "Khushūʿ belongs to the heart, whereas khuḍūʿ applies to the limbs.", "reasons": "Tabatabai states the reverse distinction from sources that make khushūʿ broader; Qurtubi and Qatada likewise place the praiseworthy state in the heart with natural outward signs."}, {"id": "2:45/q16/p4", "position": "Khushūʿ is bodily humility, while khuḍūʿ is softness and compliance attributable to the heart.", "reasons": "Baydawi reverses the customary body/heart allocation; Kashshaf defines khuḍūʿ through softened speech."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q17", "question": "What conduct counts as genuine humility?", "turns_on": "Whether an outward pose expresses an inward state or is staged for people.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q17/p1", "position": "Inward fear and justice issue naturally in composure, kindness, equal treatment, and attentive prayer.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites Nakha'i on treating high and low equally in right, Ali on a humble heart, gentleness and not turning during prayer, and Sahl on every hair responding, with 39:23. Bursevi repeats these; the early generations tried to conceal outward signs. Ibn Ashur says true humility is a disciplined readiness to accept God's command and rejects restricting it to reverence while already standing in prayer (23:1–2)."}, {"id": "2:45/q17/p2", "position": "Affected outward signs to gain esteem are false humility.", "reasons": "Al-A'mash rebukes Sufyan for reducing it to coarse clothing, food, or bowed head; Umar tells a youth to raise his head and strikes a theatrical mourner in another report. Qurtubi calls such display hypocrisy; Bursevi cites Umar's loud speech, brisk walk and forceful strike as compatible with true asceticism."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q18", "question": "Which reports illustrate resorting to prayer in trouble?", "turns_on": "The differing agents, afflicted people, events, and report details.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q18/p1", "position": "The Prophet prayed when distressed.", "reasons": "Hudhayfa's report is transmitted by Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Durr and Alusi; Ibn Kathir names Ahmad and Abu Dawud. A disconnected version through Hudhayfa's relative describes him cloaked and praying on the night of the Confederates. Some versions add fasting; reports also describe his prayer through the night of Badr while others slept, mosque refuge on windy nights, eclipse prayers, and earlier prophets praying in fear. The Prophet also called prayer his eye's comfort and summoned Bilal to refresh them with it."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p2", "position": "The Prophet directed a person in pain to pray, calling prayer healing.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Kathir name Abu Hurayra lying on his stomach with abdominal pain; Mawardi's version names Salman and cold. These are distinct recipient details."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p3", "position": "Ibn Abbas prayed two rak'as after news of a relative's death and recited this verse.", "reasons": "Tabari, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Durr say his brother Qutham; Qurtubi notes brother Qutham or daughter, while Durr separately reports his son and Bursevi his daughter. Accounts vary on length of sitting, stepping from the road, return formula, and words of praise."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p4", "position": "Ali prayed and recited the verse when troubled.", "reasons": "An al-Kafi report through al-Sadiq gives this practice; another report says Ali prayed and supplicated through Badr's night."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p5", "position": "Al-Sadiq directs someone struck by worldly grief to wash, pray two units in the mosque, and supplicate.", "reasons": "Tabarsi states no grading; Tabatabai infers fasting and prayer are recommended in calamities from associated reports."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p6", "position": "Umm Kulthum sought aid through prayer when her husband Abdurrahman appeared near death.", "reasons": "The Durr report says he later recounted two angels' summons and a third angel's assurance of blessed fate from before birth, and lived another month."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p7", "position": "Ubadah, dying, ordered companions to wash, pray in the mosque, seek forgiveness, then hasten his burial.", "reasons": "The Durr transmits this instruction and his prohibition of mourning."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p8", "position": "A grave affliction calls for fasting.", "reasons": "Al-Kafi and al-Ayyashi reports through al-Sadiq and Abu al-Hasan identify patience with fasting and tell the afflicted to fast; Tabatabai notes al-Ayyashi transmits the substance of both reports."}, {"id": "2:45/q18/p9", "position": "The verse was revealed about Ali, Uthman ibn Maz'un, Ammar ibn Yasir and their companions.", "reasons": "Tabatabai relays Ibn Shahrashub's report from al-Baqir."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q19", "question": "How does the command connect with its context and other verses?", "turns_on": "How the verse's command and prayer focus relate to the immediate discourse and parallel passages.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q19/p1", "position": "It remedies the difficult prior Israelite commands and renews the earlier order to pray.", "reasons": "Tabari links endurance and glorification at 20:130; Ibn Ashur links 2:43 and explains that confidence in the addressees encourages compliance. Alusi, Baydawi and Kur'an Yolu connect it to abandoning error, accepting the Prophet, prayer and alms despite status and wealth. Ibn Ashur says the passage also indirectly praises Muslims."}, {"id": "2:45/q19/p2", "position": "It parallels 2:153 and other Qur'anic links between patience, prayer and steadfastness.", "reasons": "Razi notes the believers' command at 2:153; Study Quran also cites 12:18, 16:127, 23:111, 70:5, 90:17 and 103:3. Tabatabai sees Jacob completing patience with trust in 12:18 and 12:83. Ibn Ashur relates patience to 103:1–3, 32:24, 7:137 and 2:153."}, {"id": "2:45/q19/p3", "position": "The close here turns to prayer because 2:43 commanded it; 2:153 turns to patience because trials and martyrdom follow.", "reasons": "Samarrai compares 2:43 with 2:154–156 and the patient response in 2:156."}, {"id": "2:45/q19/p4", "position": "Prayer is understood as joined to faith in Muhammad for the scriptural leaders.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Zajjaj say that this combination, opposed by love of leadership, explains the difficulty."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q20", "question": "What does the following description of meeting and returning to God add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q20/p1", "position": "It explains the humble through firm expectation of resurrection, judgment, and reward.", "reasons": "Muqatil says they know they will meet and return for recompense. Ibn Ashur takes ẓann as conviction, citing Aws ibn Hajar and Durayd ibn al-Simmah; meeting and return can mean resurrection and judgment or vision and reward, with 2:37, 2:223 and 6:31. Bursevi says ẓann can mean certainty, while Harali allows weaker hope beneath certainty."}, {"id": "2:45/q20/p2", "position": "The description distinguishes the humble from people who lack faith in recompense.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Bursevi describe hypocrites and ostentatious worshippers as experiencing only difficulty without hope of reward or fear of punishment."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q21", "question": "What is meant by divine patience in the associated reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q21/p1", "position": "God's ṣabr means forbearance and delay of deserved punishment.", "reasons": "Qurtubi cites the Bukhari report through Abu Musa: people attribute a child to God yet He pardons and provides; scholars including Ibn Furak say this attribute appears in hadith, not Qur'an, and al-Sabur is an emphatic name. Bursevi repeats the report with 'cure and provide' and says a sinner feels less safe under Patient than Forbearing."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q22", "question": "What inward or allegorical readings are attached to the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the outward practices signify interior states or specific sacred persons and eras.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q22/p1", "position": "Patience leaves all besides God; prayer abides in His unseen presence.", "reasons": "Sulami's Iraqis, Qushayri, Qashani and Najmiyya describe ego restraint, proper standing, divine manifestations, and continuing service when awe threatens to absorb the servant; Qushayri says easing the unveiling restores ordinary duties."}, {"id": "2:45/q22/p2", "position": "Patience and prayer are allegorically related to the Prophet and Ali as channels of help.", "reasons": "Tabatabai infers this from reports recommending fasting and prayer in calamity and identifying humble worshippers with the Messenger and Ali."}, {"id": "2:45/q22/p3", "position": "The verse alludes to afternoon prayer, the final Prophet's era, and servitude rather than kingship.", "reasons": "Biqai says those expecting prophetic kingship find the condition of servitude difficult until humbled."}]}

"id": "2:45/q23", "question": "What pressures make this command necessary?", "turns_on": "The sources name personal attachment and public wrongdoing as different pressures.", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q23/p1", "position": "Attachment to worldly comfort or status makes obedience difficult.", "reasons": "Biqai reports that the Prophet asked the grieving Umar whether he was content for others to have this world while they had the Hereafter; this illustrates the preceding demand to surrender worldly attachment."}, {"id": "2:45/q23/p2", "position": "Public moral decline and promotion of falsehood bring suffering and divine anger.", "reasons": "Elmalili says this is a fundamental source of human suffering, though God's mercy remains universal."}]}
{"id": "2:45/q24", "question": "What does practicing prayer effectively require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:45/q24/p1", "position": "Enduring its duties, distraction, sincerity, attention, and reverence.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says seek help by joining patience to prayer and bearing its hardships and etiquette; Biqai says prayer's greatness demands leaving self-interest and accepting the lowliness of servitude before God."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q01", "question": "How does this recollection connect with the surrounding account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q01/p1", "position": "It continues the dialogue with Israel and recalls another favor after the calf episode.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan links it to Moses' speech in 2:54; Razi calls the death and revival a sixth favor permitting repentance and reward. Kur'an Yolu says this passage condenses the longer history in 7:141–162 while adding these details."}, {"id": "2:55/q01/p2", "position": "It is a warning and consolation through the ancestors' repeated resistance.", "reasons": "Tabari compares their earlier rebellions (5:24; 7:161); Wahidi, Jishumi, Tabarsi, Razi and Biqai apply the pattern to Jews resisting Muhammad, and Razi says it consoles him, explains why signs are withheld, and why scriptural learning need not lead to belief. Razi adds that Muhammad's accurate unstudied narration proves revelation; Zajjaj and Biqai connect resurrection to disputants who denied it."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q02", "question": "Who said this to Moses, and why are later Israelites addressed?", "turns_on": "The competing identifications give different numbers and scope to the speaking group; later collective address may reflect ancestral or communal responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q02/p1", "position": "Moses' seventy selected companions spoke; the later community is addressed through its ancestors.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi and many commentators identify the seventy; Ibn Kathir says this is the dominant contextual account. Jishumi says the addressees followed and approved their ancestors; Elmalılı grounds collective attribution in communal responsibility. Abu Hayyan rejects a claim of unanimity because other identifications exist."}, {"id": "2:55/q02/p2", "position": "All Israelites except those whom God protected spoke.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's report is repeated by Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi; it differs from identification with the selected seventy."}, {"id": "2:55/q02/p3", "position": "Ten thousand Israelites spoke.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf and Baydawi transmit this number alongside the seventy report; Alusi repeats it."}, {"id": "2:55/q02/p4", "position": "Those who stayed with Aaron and did not worship the calf spoke.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan records this further identification."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q03", "question": "When and why were the men selected for the mountain meeting?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over whether the selection and demand preceded or followed the calf worshippers' self-killing, and whether an earlier appointed meeting is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q03/p1", "position": "They were selected after the calf episode to seek pardon, before the self-killing repentance was completed.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq says Moses destroyed the calf, took seventy to hear God, and only after their restoration received the command that repentance required mutual killing. Tha'labi, Mawardi, Wahidi, Baghawi and the dominant chronology in Ibn Atiyya associate selection with seeking pardon; Ibn Atiyya prefers this chronology."}, {"id": "2:55/q03/p2", "position": "They were selected after Israel had repented by mutual killing.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi says seventy survivors sought pardon, demanded vision, were revived, then asked to be prophets and were made prophets; Ibn Zayd places the demand after repentance and before rejection of the tablets and the raised mountain. Bursevi distinguishes this second selection from an earlier group after Pharaoh drowned."}, {"id": "2:55/q03/p3", "position": "They were selected after the sea crossing for the appointed meeting.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqash and others place the selection then; Ibn Atiyya prefers the later calf chronology."}, {"id": "2:55/q03/p4", "position": "The verse leaves the chronology and whether the seekers worshipped the calf unresolved.", "reasons": "Razi says neither of the two reported chronologies, nor the seekers' prior calf worship, is settled by this verse; Elmalılı also leaves timing open."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q04", "question": "What did the group do and experience before making the demand?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q04/p1", "position": "At Sinai they prepared themselves, heard God address Moses, then demanded open sight.", "reasons": "Tha'labi has seventy fasting and purifying themselves, asking to hear God, prostrating in the cloud, and hearing the command to worship God alone. Baghawi adds a screen against Moses' light and a reminder of deliverance from Egypt. Ibn Atiyya reports sixty elders plus ten youths who matured overnight, seventy chosen from seventy-two with Joshua and Talut left behind at equal reward, three days' abstinence and bathing, Aaron left in charge, then cloud, light and prostration. Al-Suddi says some later altered what they heard (2:75)."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q05", "question": "What does calling Moses by his bare name convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q05/p1", "position": "It is a singular vocative.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi state the grammatical form."}, {"id": "2:55/q05/p2", "position": "It shows discourtesy toward the prophet.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan contrasts 24:63's instruction about addressing Muhammad; Biqai says they used a bare name despite witnessing God's honor to Moses."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q06", "question": "What belief were they withholding?", "turns_on": "The disputed object of belief is Moses' prophethood, the particular revelation he brought, or the completeness of existing faith.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q06/p1", "position": "They refused to affirm Moses as a truthful commissioned prophet.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Wahidi Wajiz, Tabarsi and Razi explain this as withholding trust in Moses himself; al-Asamm and Tabarsi specify his prophetic commission. Baydawi includes it as one option."}, {"id": "2:55/q06/p2", "position": "They withheld acceptance of Moses' account of God, Torah, or divine commands.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi mention God's attributes; Ibn Zayd makes the Torah's authenticity decisive. Bursevi combines the book, Moses hearing speech, and the command to follow. Abu Hayyan cites 12:17 for trusting what Moses brought, and Biqai distinguishes detailed teachings from basic faith by 9:61. Alusi says they already believed Moses."}, {"id": "2:55/q06/p3", "position": "They denied complete faith until the further sign.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan compares a hadith requiring supreme love of the Prophet for full faith; Alusi cites loving for one's fellow believer what one loves for oneself."}, {"id": "2:55/q06/p4", "position": "Their refusal conditions true faith on direct witnessing, in an inward reading.", "reasons": "Qashani reads Moses' guidance as leading toward direct witnessing."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q07", "question": "How does the lām in 'believe you' work?", "turns_on": "The construction may supply acknowledgment as the verb's sense or make Moses' claim the cause or purpose of belief.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q07/p1", "position": "It marks affirmation or acknowledgment of Moses.", "reasons": "Qurtubi glosses believe/affirm; Baydawi gives this sense; Abu Hayyan and Samīn derive it from acknowledgment, including the unstated claim about Torah or speech, with 3:81 cited."}, {"id": "2:55/q07/p2", "position": "It is causal or purposive: belief because of Moses' claim.", "reasons": "Baydawi gives 'because of what you say'; Abu Hayyan and Samīn likewise allow causation, while Alusi allows purpose."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q08", "question": "What does īmān mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q08/p1", "position": "It means assent or belief.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites the brothers' statement in 12:17 as a parallel."}]}

{"id": "2:55/q12", "question": "How is narā Allāh read with imāla?", "turns_on": "The disagreement is whether temporary loss of the alif also removes the phonetic basis of its imāla, and which route is transmitted.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q12/p1", "position": "Imāla of the rāʾ is transmitted in connected reading.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr inclines the hamza's fatḥa toward yāʾ to incline the alif; al-Fārisi says an open rāʾ or emphatic consonant does not prevent it, citing saqā and ṣafā. Ibn al-Jazarī refers back to those routes."}, {"id": "2:55/q12/p2", "position": "When liaison elides the alif, the known reading leaves the rāʾ uninclined.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisi reports the standard Abū ʿAmr treatment; Aḥmad ibn Mūsā says it is the known one. Sibawayh supports restoring fatḥa when the target of imāla disappears."}, {"id": "2:55/q12/p3", "position": "Imāla may remain even when the alif drops temporarily.", "reasons": "Ibn Mūsā transmits this from ʿAbd al-Wārith and ʿAbbās for Abū ʿAmr; Abū al-Ḥasan accepts both Arabic treatments. {"id": "2:55/q13", "question": "How is the divine-name lām pronounced after imāla?", "turns_on": "The preceding imāla is neither a pure kasra nor a pure fatḥa.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q13/p1", "position": "Both heavy and light lām are transmitted.", "reasons": "The performance authorities reason respectively that no pure kasra or no pure fatḥa precedes; Ibn al-Ḥājib prefers the light original pronunciation because neither pure fatḥa nor ḍamma precedes and compares the light rāʾ at pause. {"id": "2:55/q14", "question": "What does jahratan add to the requested sight or speech?", "turns_on": "The adverb may attach to 'see' or to 'said'; the former specifies bodily vision and the latter publicity of speech.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q14/p1", "position": "It demands open, unobstructed ocular sight of God.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba excludes sleep; Tabari derives the disclosure from cleaning a muddy well and cites al-Farazdaq, Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi and Ibn Zayd; Tha'labi cites poetry; Mawardi compares loud recitation and public sin; Wahidi cites Abu Zayd and al-Aʿsha. Tabarsi, Qurtubi, Razi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi exclude dream and inward perception. Biqai contrasts public unveiling with private nearness."}, {"id": "2:55/q14/p2", "position": "It describes the demand being voiced openly.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Abu Ubayda take it with the utterance; Tabarsi and Abu Hayyan report this, Qurtubi says it requires reordering, while Samīn disputes that syntactic objection. Alusi emphasizes that the speakers showed no hesitation."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q15", "question": "What is the accusative construction of jahratan?", "turns_on": "The analyses differ over which verb or participant governs the accusative and whether the noun names a kind of sight.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q15/p1", "position": "It is a verbal noun denoting a kind of seeing or an adverbial circumstance of vision or seers.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Wahidi, Jishumi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Samīn, Bursevi and Alusi describe these analyses. Wahidi calls it faʿla from jahr used for an object; Abu Hayyan prefers manner or kind; Samīn prefers the verbal noun. The plural jāhir analysis supports a circumstance of the seers."}, {"id": "2:55/q15/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial to 'you said' or to the speakers.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya also mentions attachment to 'we believe'; Samīn calls that senseless. Abū al-Baqāʾ takes it with qaltum; Samīn says ordinary order can support that without Qurtubi's transposition."}, {"id": "2:55/q15/p3", "position": "It is circumstantial to God as the object seen: manifest and uncovered.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Samīn and Bursevi state this alternative."}, {"id": "2:55/q15/p4", "position": "It is a cognate accusative with an omitted verb 'you disclosed openly'.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ supplies the omitted verb."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q16", "question": "How is jahratan vocalized?", "turns_on": "They are dialectal vowel forms, with an additional possible plural analysis for the open-hāʾ form.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q16/p1", "position": "The general reading leaves hāʾ quiescent.", "reasons": "Tha'labi and Jishumi identify the common form; other commentators treat it as the base alongside the variant."}, {"id": "2:55/q16/p2", "position": "Ibn Abbas and others open the hāʾ with fatḥa.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samīn and Alusi report it; Sahl ibn Shuʿayb and Humayd ibn Qays are also named. It may be a dialectal faʿala verbal noun like ghalaba or a plural of jāhir. Ibn Atiyya says Basrans attest the fatḥa near a guttural after an open syllable, while Kufans allow it by analogy."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q17", "question": "Can God be seen, and in what manner or time?", "turns_on": "The central dispute is whether condemnation of this demand proves vision impossible, or punishes the circumstances and manner of a request for a possible afterlife vision.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q17/p1", "position": "Divine vision is impossible; visual perception would entail bodily quality or direction.", "reasons": "Jishumi reasons that anything seen has body, color or likeness and says even a bare request is condemned; Zamakhshari says Moses refuted directed vision. Al-Balkhi adduces 4:153; Qadi Abd al-Jabbar and Abu al-Husayn argue punishment for the request proves impossibility, citing 2:61, 4:153 and 25:21. These arguments are attributed to Muʿtazila and other sects."}, {"id": "2:55/q17/p2", "position": "God can be seen without likeness or modality, especially by believers in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Qurtubi invokes Moses' own request; Abu Hayyan cites abundant sound hadith and describes sight without direction, facing, color, form or corporeality. Razi says condemnation of a possible request proves no impossibility, since the paired book and angel requests in 4:153 and 25:21 are possible. Baydawi and Bursevi allow afterlife vision and some prophetic worldly vision; Elmalılı says God can create capable eyes but present eyes cannot encompass Him. Biqai cites the Prophetic promise and 75:22–23."}, {"id": "2:55/q17/p3", "position": "Vision without anthropomorphic likeness is itself unbelief.", "reasons": "Abu al-Qasim states this stricter judgment; Jishumi also says vision with anthropomorphic likeness is unbelief, while Abu Ali and Abu Hashim distinguish the nonanthropomorphic case."}, {"id": "2:55/q17/p4", "position": "God would be seen as a body from above or in an image.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes bodily direction to Karramiyya and image to anthropomorphists."}, {"id": "2:55/q17/p5", "position": "It remains unsettled whether the punishment condemns vision itself.", "reasons": "Razi explicitly rejects the inference from punishment to impossibility; Tabarsi connects Moses' request in 7:143 to his people's request, saying Torah adherents agree he requested vision only once and on their behalf."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q18", "question": "Does God see Himself?", "turns_on": "Abu Hayyan reports three positions on divine self-perception.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q18/p1", "position": "Most Muʿtazilites say He does not.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this view."}, {"id": "2:55/q18/p2", "position": "Another Muʿtazilite group says He does.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this alternative."}, {"id": "2:55/q18/p3", "position": "Al-Kaʿbi and al-Najjar say He sees neither Himself nor anything else.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan distinguishes this from the other two Muʿtazilite views."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q19", "question": "Why was the demand punished?", "turns_on": "The explanations distinguish the object and possibility of the requested vision from the group's defiance after established proof and from alternative prior offenses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q19/p1", "position": "It was obstinate refusal of a proven messenger and a demand for needless further proof.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Razi say a messenger must be believed once miracles establish him; Jishumi calls a post-proof refusal unbelief. Moses requested from faith and longing, unlike the group's doubting denial. Elmalılı connects their sensory insistence to calf worship and inability to believe unseen truth. Biqai likewise notes clear signs were already enough."}, {"id": "2:55/q19/p2", "position": "They demanded an impossible bodily or worldly sight of God.", "reasons": "Jishumi makes the bare request culpable and says punishment deterred others. Kashshaf says a body in a direction would follow; Baydawi distinguishes such sight from vision without modality. Ibn Kathir calls open vision impossible for them; Bursevi and Elmalılı confine the impossibility to their earthly condition or encompassing bodily sight. Biqai says public unveiling is for selected nearness, not rejecters."}, {"id": "2:55/q19/p3", "position": "They improperly asked Moses to show what was outside his power.", "reasons": "Ibn Furak connects the wording to 4:153

{"id": "2:55/q20", "question": "What was the ṣāʿiqa that seized them?", "turns_on": "Reports identify different physical causes; other interpreters use the term for the destructive effect or a broader class of overwhelming events.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q20/p1", "position": "It was death or a deadly punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite the raising after death in 2:56 or 39:68. Tustari gives death and destructive punishment. Ibn Abbas uses Rabi'a's verse for a deadly calamity. Razi rejects equating the thing seen with death itself."}, {"id": "2:55/q20/p2", "position": "It was fire or lightning from heaven that burned them.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi, Tha'labi, Wahidi and others give fire; Jishumi cites 13:13 and his root sense of heavenly fire. Biqai prefers fire because they watched it. Bursevi adds a sound."}, {"id": "2:55/q20/p3", "position": "It was a heavenly cry, sound, or force heard by the group.", "reasons": "Al-Rabi reports a sound; Marwan calls it a heavenly cry; Wahb says a heavenly force killed them for a day and night; Kashshaf, Baydawi and Alusi list heard hosts or a cry."}, {"id": "2:55/q20/p4", "position": "It was a quake or tremor.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq calls the killing tremor the thunderbolt; Razi and Abu Hayyan cite the rajfah parallel in 7:155 for an external cause, and Study Quran notes ṣāʿiqa has broader range than rajfah."}, {"id": "2:55/q20/p5", "position": "It names any overwhelming event or cause of death, including sound, fire, quake, terror, or loss of faculties.", "reasons": "Tabari's broad definition includes bodily harm, loss of reason or a faculty; Jishumi extends heavenly fire to punishment and cites 41:13. Razi says the object named is the cause, not death itself; Abu Hayyan prefers that view. Asad says the Qur'an specifies no physical form, though lexicographers agree on force and suddenness. Study Quran notes calamity, destruction and the analogous afflictions of ʿĀd and Thamūd."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q21", "question": "Did the strike kill them or merely stun them?", "turns_on": "The texts use death and raising for the group but waking for Moses; some reports interpret the group's episode as extreme terror or swooning.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q21/p1", "position": "They died, then were restored to complete their allotted lives.", "reasons": "Qatada and al-Rabi explicitly say this; 2:56 is cited as proof of death. Baghawi says Moses pleaded with 7:155 and they revived one by one after a day and night; Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi explain his fear of returning without them. Ibn Atiyya says their spirits departed and they were good when they left. The alternating groups report varies sequence."}, {"id": "2:55/q21/p2", "position": "They fainted or entered a near-death state and later recovered.", "reasons": "Tabari cites Moses waking in 7:143 and Jarir's comparison of a living Farazdaq; Kashshaf says Moses' own ṣaʿq was swooning. Wahb describes terror and loss of senses, with 2:56 using revival for recovery; Elmalılı makes the calamity a communal death in effect, with survivors unable to move."}, {"id": "2:55/q21/p3", "position": "Moses was struck unconscious but did not die, unlike the Israelites.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi distinguish 'awoke' for Moses in 7:143 from 'raised' for the others in 2:56; another report says he too was struck, without settling whether he died."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q22", "question": "How is ṣāʿiqa read?", "turns_on": "The two noun forms are transmitted as linguistic variants.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q22/p1", "position": "The general reading is al-ṣāʿiqa with an alif.", "reasons": "Tha'labi and Jishumi distinguish it from the shorter variant."}, {"id": "2:55/q22/p2", "position": "Umar, Uthman, Ali and others read al-ṣaʿqa without an alif.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Jishumi, Qurtubi, Ibn Atiyya and Alusi report the named readers; Qurtubi adds Ibn Muhaysin throughout the Qur'an, Abu Hayyan names ʿAmr, and Ibn Atiyya says the short noun is what comes upon a person from a thunderbolt. Kashshaf also records Ali's fa-adhkhatkum al-ṣaʿqa."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q23", "question": "What does the thunderbolt's 'taking' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q23/p1", "position": "It seized, overtook, and surrounded them by force.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives grasping by hand as the root; Alusi says it overcame and encompassed them; Biqai emphasizes whole and violent grasp."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q24", "question": "What were they looking at as the strike came?", "turns_on": "The interpretations identify the object as the approaching event, one another, its aftermath, knowledge, or an awaited vision; Elmalılı stresses the timing of the clause.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q24/p1", "position": "They watched the strike, fire, or its approaching signs and effects.", "reasons": "Tustari says they witnessed it while others learned a warning; Mawardi says they saw death; Wahidi Wajiz, Nasafi, Biqai and Bursevi say they watched descending lightning or fire. Tabarsi says signs leading to death; Baydawi allows event or effects; Razi says this made punishment more severe, and Kashshaf says they were struck by what they sought to see. Abu Hayyan and Alusi include effects visible after revival."}, {"id": "2:55/q24/p2", "position": "Some watched others being struck, died, or revived in turn.", "reasons": "Urwa ibn Ruwaym says a first group was struck while others watched, then the sequence reversed; Ibn Zayd says they watched one another. Baghawi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi also allow mutual looking; Abu Hayyan includes watching individual revivals and cites Ezra."}, {"id": "2:55/q24/p3", "position": "Looking means knowing what was happening.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi allow mental knowledge in place of ocular observation."}, {"id": "2:55/q24/p4", "position": "They were awaiting the requested vision.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan allows an Arabic sense of naẓara as waiting; Alusi calls this possible but unattested here and cites a poetic tanẓurāni only for its Arabic usage."}, {"id": "2:55/q24/p5", "position": "They stared helplessly while struck but did not view death after death.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says looking and striking are concurrent, supported by 7:155's trembling calamity, and rejects an interpretation of dead people still looking."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q25", "question": "How is 'while you looked' constructed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q25/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause concurrent with the seizing.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Elmalılı agree on the clause's basic syntax; Elmalılı also permits coordination of simultaneous events."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q26", "question": "What is the range of naẓar?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q26/p1", "position": "It is directing the eye toward a visible object, and can extend to thought or waiting.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives visual search with a sound faculty and mental extension; Alusi cites the poem for 'wait for me' as an Arabic usage."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q27", "question": "What happened afterward, and how long did the affliction last?", "turns_on": "Accounts disagree over literal death and recovery; the narrated duration is a day and night.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q27/p1", "position": "God revived them after Moses pleaded, so they could finish their remaining lives.", "reasons": "Qatada and al-Rabi state the life-span purpose; Baghawi and Ibn Ishaq report Moses' fear of returning alone and his prayer in 7:155–156; Ibn Zayd places later rejection of the tablets and the raised mountain after revival. Al-Suddi says they then requested prophethood and were made prophets."}, {"id": "2:55/q27/p2", "position": "The death or thunderstruck interval was one day and one night.", "reasons": "Wahb, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Baydawi and Abu Hayyan transmit this duration; the latter says exegetes agree."}, {"id": "2:55/q27/p3", "position": "Some recovered from severe terror rather than literal death.", "reasons": "Wahb's alternative has Moses pray and their senses return; Elmalılı says the event amounted to a people's death and rescue to renewed life."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q28", "question": "Did moral obligation remain after their revival?", "turns_on": "Whether extraordinary direct knowledge ends the conditions for accountable faith.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q28/p1", "position": "They remained obligated.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi prefers this view ascribed to Mawardi, arguing that Israel saw the falling mountain and surrounding fire yet remained accountable, as did Jonah's people; otherwise no rational person would owe worship."}, {"id": "2:55/q28/p2", "position": "Their obligation ended after direct extraordinary knowledge.", "reasons": "The rejected view says accountability depends on inferential proof, not unavoidable knowledge after witnessing such events."}]}

{"id": "2:55/q30", "question": "How does the demand relate to the other Qur'anic accounts?", "turns_on": "Whether the different descriptions and sequences refer to one meeting or separate incidents.", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q30/p1", "position": "It is the same episode as Moses' seventy in 7:155.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others link the thunderbolt with the quake and Moses' prayer; Tabarsi and Study Quran point to 4:153's demand to see God openly. {"id": "2:55/q31", "question": "Why is the punishment's agent left unspoken?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q31/p1", "position": "The passage foregrounds God's blessings, so punishment is attributed to the thunderbolt.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says God is the actual sender, but explicit divine naming at this point could overwhelm the audience's joy; encouragement predominates over warning."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q32", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the demand and strike?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q32/p1", "position": "Direct witnessing surpasses mediated faith, and the strike is annihilation in divine self-disclosure.", "reasons": "Qashani reads refusal as remaining short of true faith until direct witnessing, and the thunderbolt as death in disclosure of the Essence while they observe."}, {"id": "2:55/q32/p2", "position": "Reverent gaze at the Divine Essence leads to majesty and then confession of helplessness.", "reasons": "Al-Sulami reports a Baghdadi saying the gazer is clothed in might and majesty and seeks refuge in repentance."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q33", "question": "How is the nūn of nuʾmina pronounced before laka?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q33/p1", "position": "Abū ʿAmr assimilates the nūn into the lām.", "reasons": "Samīn says the two sounds are close."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q34", "question": "What does the divine name Allah convey here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q34/p1", "position": "It conveys divine greatness and the impropriety of their demand.", "reasons": "Biqai contrasts the name with 'Lord' in 75:22–23, which accompanies attained vision; Allah here evokes the unseen and the group's loss."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q35", "question": "Did the seventy actually see God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q35/p1", "position": "They did not see Him.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir rejects the People of the Book's claim that they did, since Moses himself requested vision and was denied."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q36", "question": "How is al-ṣāʿiqa parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q36/p1", "position": "It is the nominative subject of the verb.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives this iʿrāb."}]}
{"id": "2:55/q37", "question": "Where else does Alusi direct the reader for this episode?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:55/q37/p1", "position": "To his later discussion in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.", "reasons": "Alusi points ahead to his treatment around 7:155."}]}
{"id": "2:61/q01", "question": "Who is addressed and how are later Israelites included?", "turns_on": "Whether the speech addresses ancestors directly or includes descendants through shared identity and approval.", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q01/p1", "position": "Israel across generations is meant", "reasons": "TAB-FULL (من قال إنها مصر فرعون): Those arguing for Pharaoh's Egypt cite the statement that Israel inherited Egypt's gardens and goods, reasoning that inheritance would be of no benefit unless some Israelites went there. TAB-FULL (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd identifies the people punished here as the Israelite Jews, explicitly distinguishing them from Egypt’s Copts. WAHIDI-BASIT (الفراء): Although Jews in Muhammad’s time did not personally kill the prophets, God calls them killers because they supported the earlier killers; the same collective attribution occurs in 5:81. TABRISI: The addressees of the recollection are the Israelites' forebears. TABRISI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Israelites divided 500 years after Moses, when captive-born offspring had become numerous, and divided again 200 years after Jesus.
